name: Annual land-cover products as an independent cross-check

identity.method_name: Three independent land-cover products used as cross-checks: Google Dynamic World V1 (near-real-time, per-scene, 10 m), ESA WorldCover (2020 and 2021 editions, 10 m), and Esri/Impact Observatory Annual Land Cover / Land Use Land Cover Time Series (2017-2025, 10 m)
identity.core_idea: All three are pre-trained deep-learning land-cover classifiers applied globally to Sentinel-2 (and, for WorldCover, also Sentinel-1) imagery, each producing per-pixel class labels at 10 m resolution -- finer than the project's own 20 m grid. Dynamic World runs a fully-convolutional neural network independently on every individual Sentinel-2 scene (near-real-time, no temporal compositing), producing a 9-class probability map (water, trees, grass, flooded_vegetation, crops, shrub_and_scrub, built, bare, snow_and_ice) per scene. ESA WorldCover and the Esri/Impact Observatory product instead build one composited map per calendar year from many scenes, giving a single annual label rather than a per-date one. All three are candidate independent cross-checks on the project's own MNDWI/NDVI-derived water and vegetation masks, but all three are still optical, Sentinel-2-trained classifiers, so their independence from the project's own method is architectural (different model, different training labels) rather than sensor-level (same underlying imagery in the Dynamic World and Esri cases).
identity.official_dataset_ids: GOOGLE/DYNAMICWORLD/V1 (Google Earth Engine); ESA/WorldCover/v100 (2020 edition) and ESA/WorldCover/v200 (2021 edition) (Google Earth Engine, also ESA WorldCover portal esa-worldcover.org and AWS Open Data registry-opendata.aws/esa-worldcover-vito); Esri 10m Annual Land Use Land Cover (2017-2025), Earth Engine asset ID projects/sat-io/open-datasets/landcover/ESRI_Global-LULC_10m_TS (community catalog / sat-io project asset, NOT in Google's own curated Earth Engine Data Catalog namespace), produced by Impact Observatory for Esri and also distributed via Esri Living Atlas / ArcGIS Online. A separate single-year Esri product, projects/sat-io/open-datasets/landcover/ESRI_Global-LULC_10m, covers 2020 only and uses a slightly different 10-class legend; the multi-year time series product is the one relevant to this item's 2017-2025 claim.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Data-source used as an independent cross-check layer, exactly as with GSW (D3) -- not a training-label generator, but external evidence against which the project's own water_ha and vegetation classifications can be compared for agreement or systematic divergence. Cost is near-zero (Earth Engine queries) except for the interpretive work of reconciling class definitions across four different legends (the project's own MNDWI/NDVI binary rule, Dynamic World's 9 classes, WorldCover's 11 classes, Esri's 9-class 2023+ legend).
fit_to_project.input_required: The existing lake polygon and target date(s)/year(s); all three products are queried directly from Google Earth Engine (two natively in the main catalog, the Esri time series via a community/sat-io project asset that must be loaded with its full path rather than a short catalog name). No new imagery needs to be acquired.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: yes-if-reframed for the two annual products (WorldCover, Esri), which naturally produce one label-composition value per lake per year -- up to 42 rows aligning with the existing table, capped by WorldCover's 2-year coverage (2020, 2021 only) to at most 6 lakes x 2 years = 12 usable rows. Dynamic World is different: because it runs per-scene, it can in principle be matched to the project's own 7 specific Sentinel-2 acquisition dates (one per lake-year), giving up to 42 date-matched comparisons -- the only one of the three products that can be aligned this precisely to the project's existing table structure rather than an annual composite that may not correspond to the project's own acquisition date.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes for all three -- each is an independently pre-trained, independently labelled classifier, so none require the project's own ground truth (which does not exist) to be used as a cross-check.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: All three are natively 10 m, i.e. finer than, not equal to, the project's 20 m grid -- the reverse mismatch problem from GSW. This is favourable for detail but requires an explicit aggregation decision (majority class, or fractional cover of each 10 m class within each 20 m project pixel / within the lake polygon) rather than a naive 1:1 pixel comparison. All three are trained on 10 m Sentinel-2 bands, the same base sensor the project uses (resampled by the project to 20 m), so there is no cross-sensor resolution mismatch of the kind GSW has (30 m Landsat).
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: None required from the project for use as a cross-check; each product supplies its own pre-trained classification.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Directly addresses limitation (3), no real ground truth, in the same way as GSW: as independent (if imperfect) reference evidence. Dynamic World additionally offers a partial mitigation of limitation (4), one scene per year showing only the dry-season minimum, IF the project chooses to also query Dynamic World for other scene dates in the same year (Dynamic World is available for every cloud-filtered Sentinel-2 acquisition since 2015-06-27, so within-year, non-project-acquisition-date snapshots become newly available for free, something the project's own cached single-scene pipeline does not have). Does not address limitation (1) (still capped well below 42 usable comparison rows for the annual products) or limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap buildings; none of these three products are building-footprint products).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: Weakly. None of the three products have a 'drained/exposed lakebed' class; a drained lake would most likely be classified as bare/bare-ground (all three have a bare-ground class) or, in WorldCover, 'bare / sparse vegetation'. This is actually a small positive: if a project lake shows 'bare' in one of these products during a year the project also records a water-area collapse, that is modest independent corroboration that the pixels really were exposed ground rather than a threshold artefact -- but it is not a clean seasonally-dry-vs-permanently-lost distinction the way GSW's multi-decadal seasonality/recurrence layers are, because none of these three products carry more than 1-9 years of history (Esri) or a single snapshot per year (WorldCover), and Dynamic World has no built-in multi-year trend layer of its own -- any trend analysis would have to be built by the student from repeated per-scene queries.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: This is the decisive question for this item and the answer differs meaningfully by product. Dynamic World has an explicit 'flooded_vegetation' class, defined as vegetation with obvious water intermixing for a majority of the year -- this is the closest match among all data-source items in this research set to a genuine, ready-made 'floating/emergent aquatic vegetation, not open water, not dry land' category, and it is a strong independent-evidence candidate for Bellandur's 260 ha of hyacinth specifically, though it was designed for wetlands generally, not hyacinth specifically, and has not been validated against the Bellandur/Varthur macrophyte map. Esri's time-series product also carries a 'Flooded Vegetation' class (it shares Impact Observatory's Dynamic World-derived training approach and class ontology), so it likely behaves similarly. ESA WorldCover, by contrast, has NO flooded-vegetation or aquatic-macrophyte class at all -- its 11 classes are tree cover, shrubland, grassland, cropland, built-up, bare/sparse vegetation, snow/ice, permanent water bodies, herbaceous wetland, mangroves, and moss/lichen; a dense hyacinth mat would most plausibly fall into 'herbaceous wetland' or simply 'grassland'/'cropland' depending on spectral similarity, none of which is a clean hyacinth-vs-water distinction, and ESA's own validation report is known to show wetland classes as among its lowest-accuracy classes globally [verify -- exact per-class accuracy figure for herbaceous wetland was not independently re-confirmed from the primary validation report in this pass]. In short: Dynamic World and Esri give a real, if unvalidated, chance at separating hyacinth from water; WorldCover almost certainly cannot, and would likely just relabel Bellandur's hyacinth mats as 'water', 'grassland' or 'herbaceous wetland' for reasons unrelated to encroachment -- exactly the false-disagreement risk the task brief warns about.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None for any of the three. All are physical land-cover products with no cadastral or legal-boundary awareness; using them changes nothing about the non-statutory status of the OpenStreetMap lake polygon the project applies them within.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: Dynamic World: genuinely varies at the finest possible grain (every cloud-filtered Sentinel-2 scene since 2015-06-27, continuing to the present as of 2026), and can be matched to the project's own 7 specific acquisition dates -- true temporal signal, not a snapshot. Esri time series: genuinely varies year to year (2017-2025, one composite per calendar year), a real annual signal, though each year is itself a composite of many scenes so it smooths out the exact dry-season-minimum framing the project uses. ESA WorldCover: only two editions exist (2020 and 2021) using two different algorithm versions (v100 and v200) -- this is the weakest of the three on temporal granularity for THIS project, since it cannot cover 2019, or any of 2022-2025 at all, and even the 2020-to-2021 change it does show conflates real land-cover change with a documented change in classification algorithm between v100 and v200, an issue ESA's own documentation flags explicitly.

implementation.libraries: Google Earth Engine Python API (earthengine-api) or JavaScript Code Editor; geemap for visualization; for the Esri time series, the community/sat-io asset must be loaded via its full path (ee.ImageCollection('projects/sat-io/open-datasets/landcover/ESRI_Global-LULC_10m_TS')) rather than a short catalog name, since it is not in Google's first-party catalog.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable in the sense of weights the student downloads and runs -- all three are pre-computed, already-classified raster products served directly from Earth Engine. Dynamic World's underlying model is a fully-convolutional neural network trained by Google/World Resources Institute on Sentinel-2 L1C imagery at 10 m with a large crowdsourced and expert-refined label set [verify -- exact training set size and architecture should be confirmed against Brown et al. 2022, Scientific Data, doi 10.1038/s41597-022-01307-4, which could not be fully retrieved in this research pass due to a publisher login redirect]; the Esri/Impact Observatory model uses Dynamic World's own training-data lineage per the community catalog documentation found in this research; ESA WorldCover uses a separate ESA-funded classification chain combining Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2.
implementation.licence: All three are permissively licensed for academic use: ESA WorldCover is CC-BY-4.0; Esri/Impact Observatory Annual Land Cover is CC-BY-4.0; Dynamic World is released under a Creative Commons licence (CC-BY-4.0-equivalent open terms) [verify -- exact licence text should be confirmed on the Earth Engine catalog page and the Dynamic World GitHub/about page before citing formally]. All are usable at no cost within standard Earth Engine non-commercial/academic quotas.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial for all three -- Earth Engine server-side zonal reduction over 6 small lake polygons, for a handful of dates (Dynamic World) or 2-9 years (WorldCover, Esri), completes in seconds to low minutes and needs no local GPU or heavy compute; fully reproducible on a laptop with an Earth Engine account.
implementation.student_days: 1-2 student-days total for all three combined: Earth Engine access/setup (shared with the GSW item if both are pursued, since both live in Earth Engine, though the Esri asset requires locating and correctly citing its community-catalog path); writing zonal-reduction scripts for each product's class fractions per lake per available date/year; reconciling the three different class legends against the project's own binary water/vegetation categories (the most conceptually fiddly part, since 'flooded_vegetation' vs 'water' vs 'trees' must be mapped by hand to the project's water_ha and veg_ha definitions); producing comparison tables/plots, with particular attention to the Bellandur/Varthur hyacinth years.

evaluation.metrics: Class-composition agreement metrics between each product's water/flooded-vegetation/trees fraction inside each lake polygon and the project's own MNDWI/NDVI-derived water_ha and vegetation_ha, per available date; qualitative flagging of which product's classification each lake-year is 'consistent' or 'inconsistent' with, and, specifically for Bellandur/Varthur, whether each product calls the known hyacinth years 'water', 'trees', or something else (this is the single most informative comparison this item can produce).
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not a train/test split -- these are external comparison layers applied identically across all 6 lakes for whatever dates/years each product covers. Report coverage explicitly per product (Dynamic World: any of the project's 7 acquisition dates since 2015-06-27, in practice all of them; WorldCover: 2020 and 2021 only; Esri: 2019-2025 [uncertain -- confirm the exact end year of the currently published Esri time series, seen as 2017-2025 as of a May 2026 update in this research pass, verify before quoting]), so readers can see exactly which lake-years have zero, one, two or three independent land-cover cross-checks available.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Low for the raw comparison, since all three products are trained and produced entirely independently of this project. The material risk is conceptual, not statistical: because Dynamic World's and Esri's underlying training labels and imagery source (Sentinel-2) overlap with the project's own imagery source, 'agreement' between the project's MNDWI mask and Dynamic World's water class is not fully independent evidence in the strict sense -- both are ultimately reading the same underlying spectral signal, just through different classification logic (a fixed threshold vs. a trained neural network). Only WorldCover (which also ingests Sentinel-1 radar) offers a sensor-level, not just algorithm-level, independence, and it is also the product with the worst temporal coverage of the three for this project.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: None of the three products natively provide a lake-specific calibrated uncertainty interval. Dynamic World is the partial exception: it outputs per-class probability bands (not just a hard label), so a probability-weighted water/flooded-vegetation fraction, with an explicit confidence threshold, is possible and is more informative than a bare class count; WorldCover and Esri provide only hard class labels with a single global accuracy figure attached (74.4% for WorldCover v100, 76.7% for WorldCover v200; 'over 75%' average for the Esri time series [verify -- Esri's own release documentation should be checked directly for the exact year-by-year accuracy figures rather than the single averaged claim found in the community catalog summary used here]), neither of which is a Bengaluru-specific or lake-specific estimate.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable -- used as fixed external reference layers, not as a source of synthetic training data.

evidence.published_performance: Dynamic World: reported overall top-1 classification accuracy is commonly cited around the mid-70s percent range globally [verify -- this research pass could not retrieve the exact figure directly from Brown et al. 2022, Scientific Data (doi 10.1038/s41597-022-01307-4) due to a publisher authentication redirect encountered twice during this research; the figure must be confirmed from the primary paper or its Earth Engine catalog summary before being quoted in the project]. ESA WorldCover: overall accuracy 74.4% for the 2020 v100 edition and 76.7% for the 2021 v200 edition, per ESA's own validation reporting reflected in the Earth Engine catalog page and WorldCover documentation. Esri/Impact Observatory time series: 'each of the maps has an assessed average accuracy of over 75%' per the product's own release notes as summarised in the community catalog [verify -- exact per-year, per-class figures should be confirmed against Esri/Impact Observatory's own methodology and accuracy-assessment documentation rather than this single averaged claim].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: All three accuracy figures are GLOBAL averages across enormously heterogeneous land-cover types and climate zones, not scores computed for small Indian urban lakes, and certainly not for hyacinth-choked lakes specifically. A global mid-70s-to-high-70s percent accuracy figure provides essentially no information about performance on a 315 ha lake footprint that is 82% covered by dense floating vegetation (Bellandur, 260 ha hyacinth of 315 ha total in 2019) -- this is exactly the kind of unusual, non-representative land-cover configuration that a globally-averaged accuracy figure is least informative about.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No India-specific or Bengaluru-specific validation of any of the three products' water/flooded-vegetation class accuracy was found in this research pass [verify]. All three have been used in various India-wide land-cover and wetland-mapping studies as input layers (a common pattern in Indian remote-sensing literature for area statistics), but no paper validating their accuracy specifically for Bengaluru's lakes, or for hyacinth-affected water bodies, was located during this search.
evidence.evidence_recency: 2022 for the Dynamic World method paper (Brown et al., Scientific Data); 2020/2021 for the two ESA WorldCover editions and their validation reports; 2023-2026 for successive Esri/Impact Observatory time-series releases (with a stated update through 2025 as of a May 2026 release note found in this pass) [verify]. All within or close to the post-2020 evidence-recency preference.
evidence.primary_sources: Dynamic World V1, Earth Engine Data Catalog: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/GOOGLE_DYNAMICWORLD_V1 ; Brown, C.F. et al. (2022). 'Dynamic World, Near real-time global 10 m land use land cover mapping.' Scientific Data 9, 251. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01307-4 [verify -- full text could not be retrieved in this pass, redirected to publisher login]; Dynamic World project site: https://dynamicworld.app/about/ ; ESA WorldCover 10m v100 (2020): https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/ESA_WorldCover_v100 ; ESA WorldCover 10m v200 (2021): https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/ESA_WorldCover_v200 ; ESA WorldCover project/data access: https://esa-worldcover.org/en/data-access ; Esri 10m Annual Land Use Land Cover Time Series, community catalog documentation: https://gee-community-catalog.org/projects/esrilc2020/ and https://gee-community-catalog.org/projects/S2TSLULC/ [verify -- these are third-party community catalog mirrors of Esri/Impact Observatory documentation, not Esri's own primary technical/accuracy report, which should be located and cited directly (Esri Living Atlas 'Sentinel-2 Land Cover Explorer' methodology page) before final submission].

risk.failure_modes: (1) Coverage gaps differ sharply by product: WorldCover only exists for 2020 and 2021 (2 of the project's 7 years), so it is the weakest cross-check by far despite being the only one with an added Sentinel-1 radar signal; Dynamic World and Esri cover the full 2019-2025 window (or close to it) but neither has been validated locally. (2) Legend mismatch: none of the three legends map cleanly onto the project's binary water/vegetation rule, so any comparison requires a documented, defensible mapping decision (e.g., is 'herbaceous wetland' counted as water, vegetation, or its own third category?) that itself becomes a modelling choice open to challenge. (3) Shared-imagery non-independence: Dynamic World and Esri are both trained on Sentinel-2, the same sensor the project uses, so 'independent' here means independent algorithm and independent training labels, not independent sensor -- only WorldCover adds a genuinely different sensor (Sentinel-1 SAR), but at the cost of the worst temporal coverage of the three. (4) Hyacinth-specific failure: WorldCover has no flooded-vegetation class at all and will most likely mislabel the Bellandur/Varthur hyacinth mats as water, herbaceous wetland, or grassland for reasons entirely unrelated to encroachment -- if used naively as a cross-check without this caveat stated, a panel could reasonably say the disagreement it produces is meaningless noise, not a genuine independent contradiction.
risk.panel_defensibility: The strongest, most defensible claim available from this item is narrow and specific: 'Dynamic World's flooded_vegetation class, matched to our exact Sentinel-2 acquisition dates, gives us an independently-trained (though not independently-sensed) second opinion on whether Bellandur/Varthur pixels are open water, vegetation, or a distinct floating-vegetation category, for all 7 of our years; ESA WorldCover, while it adds true sensor-level independence via Sentinel-1, only exists for 2 of our 7 years and has no flooded-vegetation class at all, so we do not use it for the hyacinth question, only as a coarse water-extent sanity check for 2020-2021.' A panel asking 'is this really independent' should be met with exactly this nuance -- claiming blanket independence for all three products, without distinguishing WorldCover's radar contribution from Dynamic World/Esri's shared-Sentinel-2 lineage, would not survive scrutiny.
risk.honest_expectation: A realistic, reportable outcome is a per-lake-year table showing how each available product classifies the pixels the project calls 'water' and 'vegetation', with an explicit callout for Bellandur and Varthur showing whether Dynamic World's flooded_vegetation class picks up the hyacinth mats distinctly from open water (a genuinely informative, checkable result) and whether WorldCover instead folds them into water or wetland (a genuinely informative disagreement, but one driven by class-legend limitations, not by the products detecting something the project's method missed). A null or mixed result -- 'independent cross-checks partially validate our water mask, but none of the three, including the two most temporally complete ones, were built with hyacinth in mind, so full resolution of the vegetation confound still rests on the dedicated macrophyte-mapping literature' -- is the honest and defensible finding.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time, with Dynamic World prioritised over the other two -- it is the only one of the three that can be matched to the project's exact 7 acquisition dates, covers the full 2019-2025 window, and has a purpose-built flooded_vegetation class that is the closest ready-made proxy for the hyacinth confound among all annual/near-annual land-cover products; WorldCover is worth a light, clearly-caveated look for its 2 years of Sentinel-1-based (genuinely sensor-independent) evidence but should not be relied on for the hyacinth question since it has no flooded-vegetation class; the Esri time series is a reasonable middle option if extra corroboration is wanted but adds relatively little beyond what Dynamic World already provides given their shared training lineage.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We used Google Dynamic World, matched to our own 7 Sentinel-2 acquisition dates, as our main independent land-cover cross-check because its flooded_vegetation class can flag the Bellandur/Varthur hyacinth mats separately from open water, and we used ESA WorldCover only as a limited 2020-2021 sanity check since it adds genuine radar-based sensor independence but has no vegetation class capable of representing hyacinth at all.
